body:
**As a** pilot
**I want** a predicted flight path based on how the wind changes with height and over time
**so that** I can see where I am likely to land.

**Acceptance criteria**
- [ ] Inputs: launch position and UTC time, ascent rate (m/s), cruise altitude (ft), descent rate (m/s), total duration (min) and step size (s, default 60).
- [ ] The flight is split into ascent, cruise and descent phases from simple kinematics.
- [ ] When ascent plus descent alone would exceed the requested duration, ascent is scaled down proportionally and cruise collapses to zero — the simulation never overruns the requested duration.
- [ ] At each step, wind is interpolated linearly between the two bracketing hourly snapshots and between the two bracketing pressure levels.
- [ ] Wind direction is interpolated with a shortest-arc angular interpolation that handles the 0/360 wraparound — never a naive numeric average.
- [ ] With no wind data available, a valid trajectory with no points is returned so the UI can show an empty state rather than crash.
- [ ] Output records altitude, ordered points with elapsed minutes, data source, timestamp, duration and the rates used.
- [ ] Tests cover the wraparound case, the too-short-duration case and the no-data case explicitly.

body:
**As a** developer
**I want** one host serving both the API and the Angular app, with a fast local dev loop
**so that** we get single-origin simplicity in production without giving up hot reload while developing.

**Acceptance criteria**
- [ ] In development, `ng serve` runs with a proxy configuration forwarding `/api/*` to the ASP.NET Core host; hot module reload works.
- [ ] In production, the built Angular bundle is served from `wwwroot` by the same host as the API.
- [ ] A SPA fallback route returns `index.html` for unmatched client-side routes, while `/api/*` and `/health` continue to return real responses — a deep link refresh must not 404.
- [ ] Static assets are served with content-hashed filenames and long cache headers; `index.html` is never cached.
- [ ] Because API and app share an origin, no CORS policy is required — and this is asserted by a test so nobody adds a permissive one later.
- [ ] One `dotnet run` after `ng build` serves a fully working app.

**As a** maintainer
**I want** the Azure environment described in Bicep
**so that** it can be recreated or reviewed without clicking through the portal.

**Acceptance criteria**
- [ ] `infra/main.bicep` provisions a Linux App Service Plan, an App Service running .NET 10, an Azure SQL Database and a Storage account.
- [ ] Blob containers are created by the template: `flight-images`, `flight-tracks`, `flight-exports`, `map-cache`.
- [ ] The App Service gets a system-assigned managed identity, granted Storage Blob Data Contributor on the account and db_datareader/db_datawriter on the database — no connection secrets in app settings.
- [ ] Containers are private; no anonymous public blob access is possible.
- [ ] `infra/deploy.sh` performs an idempotent deployment; running it twice changes nothing.
- [ ] SKUs, names and region are parameters with sensible defaults, not literals.
- [ ] No secret values appear in the template or in the repository.

**As a** developer joining the project
**I want** to run `docker compose up --build` and get the API, the Angular app, a SQL Server and a blob emulator
**so that** onboarding takes minutes rather than an afternoon.

**Acceptance criteria**
- [ ] Compose starts the ASP.NET Core app, a SQL Server container (Azure SQL Edge, so it works on Apple Silicon) and Azurite for blob storage.
- [ ] The app is reachable on a documented port with the Angular frontend served from it.
- [ ] Database and blob volumes persist across restarts; a documented command resets them.
- [ ] Secrets and seed values come from a committed `.env.example` copied to a git-ignored `.env`.
- [ ] The Dockerfile is multi-stage — Node stage builds the Angular bundle, SDK stage builds .NET, runtime image contains neither.
- [ ] `README.md` documents the command and the prerequisites, and a fresh clone was verified against it.

**As a** developer
**I want** an EF Core `AppDbContext` on Azure SQL with a controlled migration path
**so that** the schema is always in step with the code.

**Acceptance criteria**
- [ ] `AppDbContext` extends `IdentityDbContext<ApplicationUser>` and is registered with the SQL Server provider.
- [ ] Connection string comes from configuration; in Azure it is resolved through managed identity rather than a password in app settings.
- [ ] Migrations are applied automatically in development, and by an explicit pipeline step in production — never silently at production startup.
- [ ] An initial migration exists and applies cleanly to an empty database.
- [ ] Retry-on-failure is enabled for transient Azure SQL faults.
- [ ] Integration tests run against a real SQL Server instance (Testcontainers or the compose-provided container), not an in-memory provider.

body:
**As a** developer
**I want** a solution split into Domain, Infrastructure and Api projects with an Angular workspace alongside
**so that** business rules stay testable and the frontend and backend can evolve independently while shipping as one deployable.

**Acceptance criteria**
- [ ] Solution contains `Nimbus.Domain`, `Nimbus.Infrastructure` and `Nimbus.Api` (ASP.NET Core Web API, .NET 10).
- [ ] An Angular workspace lives at `src/web`, generated with the Angular CLI, using standalone components and strict TypeScript.
- [x] `Nimbus.Domain` has no package or project references to EF Core, ASP.NET or any HTTP client — it holds models and service *interfaces* only.
- [x] `Nimbus.Infrastructure` references Domain; `Nimbus.Api` references both; there are no reverse references.
- [ ] Test projects exist for Domain, Infrastructure and Api and run green from `dotnet test`; `ng test` runs green for the Angular workspace.
- [ ] `.editorconfig`, nullable reference types and `TreatWarningsAsErrors` on the .NET side; ESLint and Prettier on the Angular side.
- [ ] `docs/architecture.md` states the layering rules, the frontend/backend boundary, and why they exist.

**Notes**
The FlightPrep POC let business services live in the web project because they needed `DbContext`. With an API boundary there is no excuse for that here — those services belong in Infrastructure behind Domain interfaces.
